newsitem.title: USA: U.S. refiners await foreign deliveries into NYMEX.
newsitem.headline: U.S. refiners await foreign deliveries into NYMEX.

text.p: U.S. refiners on Tuesday were expecting some two million barrels of foreign crude to be delivered into the NYMEX, an unusual event that some suggested was a bearish market sign.
A combination of Nigerian Bonny Light and North Sea Brent crude were likely to be delivered against the May contract, which expired on Tuesday, traders said.
Physical delivery of foreign crude on NYMEX contracts is a rare event as it is usually uneconomic and is considered the option of last resort, traders said.
Market sources said trading houses Vitol and Phibro were likely to deliver at least 700,000 barrels and 500,000 barrels, respectively, of Bonny Light, although this could not be confirmed.
ARCO was also strongly rumored to be delivering the Nigerian crude into the exchange. Company officials declined to comment.

Meanwhile, Northridge Energy Marketing Corp, a subsidiary of TransCanada Pipelines Ltd., was seen as very likely to deliver one 500,000 barrel cargo of Brent, a trade source familiar with the company's marketing operations said.

Exchange for Physical (EFPs) deals, which allow a buyer or seller to swap a futures for a physical position, were fetching a flat price to a premium of four cents on Tuesday, down from plus six to 12 cents in recent weeks, as traders wound down their flurry to escape paper positions that might give them a crude other than the benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing after today's expiry.
EFPs are usually dealt at a flat price, traders said.

Companies electing to deliver physical crude into the hub at Cushing, Oklahoma can choose to deliver a number of domestic or foreign grades but must give notice to the NYMEX by 1400 EDT/1900 GMT the day after expiry, the source said.
If a company receives Brent instead of WTI, it would receive a fixed discount of 30 cents per barrel to compensate for the differing crude qualities.
Bonny Light would require the company to pay a premium of 60 cents per barrel.
Separately, renewed unrest in Nigeria has resulted in two- to three-day delays in Bonny Light shipments, traders said.
Royal Dutch/Shell declared force majeure on Monday on Bonny exports because workers of a contracting firm that handles the berthing and loading of tankers have gone on strike.
A trading house sold a Bonny Light cargo to a Gulf Coast refiner on Tuesday at around dated Brent plus $1.93 a barrel for end-May delivery, trders said.
